| [CLAIM-600](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-600.md) v3 | Transient support can be withdrawn safely when it starts a process that keeps itself going on a flux that will stay available, when it is large enough to carry the supported party past any threshold that process has, when the threat it stood in for has gone, and when the party could do the work and did it throughout, in each subtask it must later do alone and not only in its role as a whole, at no more effort than it could bear, and, where the capacity is cumulative and its field moves fast, kept doing it after withdrawal; inputs the party cannot produce must stay supplied as a standing part of the arrangement, support that fails these leaves dependence or decay, and persistence after withdrawal is needed to tell which, though slow reversion can mimic it | The assistant's, at the owner's request of 2026-11-05 to characterize "what differentiates transient support that induces dependency and is hazardous to remove from transient support that builds new capabilities and is safe to remove", with reintroduction and ecological recovery proposed as cases. It draws together the branch's three domains: DNA origami, aid and development, and ecology. Three conditions decide it. First, the support starts a self-sustaining process on an ambient flux instead of doing the upkeep. Planted tree islands, weeded for 2.5 years, kept their advantage to 16–18 years because established trees keep drawing seed dispersers (Holl et al.; Schubert et al.). Supplied repair, by contrast, never becomes optional ([CLAIM-597](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-597.md)). Second, the threat it stood in for is gone. Conservation-reliant species stay reliant while fire is suppressed or habitat threats persist (Mussmann et al.; Brown et al.). Third, the party did the work throughout. Support that does the work wears capacity down by disuse ([CLAIM-558](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-558.md)), by slack effort (Ostrom et al.) or by selection for the supported conditions, which costs hatchery steelhead fitness in the wild within one generation (Christie et al.). Captive-bred translocated stock shows negative population growth (Morris et al.). Persistence must be shown after withdrawal: impact at exit and judged success both overstate it. Revised the same day after two counterpoints the owner asked for. Evidence against the lazy-poor stereotype finds no slack effort in poor households: cash transfers barely change work, and one-off graduation packages raise it. So that route is confined to help that is assured and permanent. A household asset threshold (Balboni et al.) adds a condition on size: support too small decays with no dependence at all. Urban development adds three cautions. Some public inputs are a standing part of a coproduced service (Evans; Watson). Forty years of persistence can be slow reversion (Kline and Moretti). And a place can last while the people it served are dispersed (Collins and Shester; LaVoice). The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Active |
| [CLAIM-601](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-601.md) v2 | A savings buffer is a stock of time: where shocks must be absorbed or a household is ruined, an investment that pays only after a delay is worth taking only above a buffer that rises with the delay, so households with the same preferences decline profitable delayed investments below it, a choice that reads as impatience and is the right policy for survival by a deadline; covering needs through the delay buys the time | The assistant's, after the owner read Haushofer and Fehr's finding, that deprivation produces short-sighted choices, as decision-making under a resource constraint: "deprivation induces added time pressure to the decision making process." | [CLAIM-603](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-603.md) | A capability lost because another reliably supplies it is the Black Queen's loss, favoured to the one who loses it, and whether it is dependency or division of labour is decided by the supply, not the loss: one-way supply set from outside, as aid is, leaves a dependence that nothing in the dependent's dynamics limits and that withdrawal punishes, while reciprocal loss, each partner supplying what the other gave up, leaves interdependence, so the aim framed as self-sufficiency is better framed as reciprocity | The assistant's, on the owner's remark of 2026-11-05 that "assured help makes recipients lose skill" sounds "closely related to niche differentiation and specialization phenomena". The record holds the biology. On the Black Queen Hypothesis ([THEORY-1048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1048.md)) a cell that stops making a leaky public good saves its cost while others still supply it, so the loss is favoured to the individual and spreads. Buchnera ([THEORY-1103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1103.md)) has lost the genes its host covers and kept those its host lacks. The Samaritan's dilemma has the same logic (Ostrom et al.), and Azam, Devarajan and O'Connell's recipient is better off in the high-aid state. The loss itself is not the pathology. What differs is the supply. A Black Queen loss stops by itself when helpers grow rare, because the helpers are the same population. Aid is set from outside and does not fall as dependence grows, so nothing stops the loss short of what aid covers, and withdrawal returns the cost ([CLAIM-602](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-602.md)). Buchnera's loss runs both ways, and the result is interdependence. A state that taxes its citizens (Moore) is in the same position: it lost nothing, it exchanges. After the owner linked the claim to the gift economy of Burning Man, readings of Mauss, of St John on Burning Man and of Heins, Unrau and Avram added two things. One-way supply costs the receiver standing as well as capacity: in Mauss the unreturned gift makes its receiver inferior. And the return need not go back to the giver: it can travel round a circuit, as Mauss's do, or out to a whole community, as Burning Man's is meant to, and both sit beside a demand for self-reliance. The wording is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [CLAIM-605](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-605.md) v2 | Where capacity is learned by doing, decays with disuse and needs capacity already present to grow, support that does the work has a deadline after which withdrawal no longer restores capacity, and a slow taper of such support is worse than an abrupt cut because it holds practice down long enough to cross the threshold; support that covers only what the party cannot yet do needs no taper but cannot lift a party already below the threshold | The assistant's, filling gaps the supplied-maintenance filing left, at the owner's request of 2026-11-05 to "proceed systematically filling all of those identified gaps". [CLAIM-602](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-602.md) modelled crowding out with no threshold, so capacity always regrew from a seed. Its own limits named the threshold case, Azam et al.'s trap. Here learning by doing needs capacity already present, dC/dt = λPC(1 − C) − μC. With λ = 1, μ = 0.3 and τ = 1.5, a party alone keeps C = 0.7, and C below 0.276 decays to nothing. The model gives three results. Support that does all the work has a deadline: after ln(0.7/0.276)/0.3 = 3.10 time units capacity has crossed the threshold, and withdrawal no longer restores it. Tapering such support is worse the slower it is: from C = 0.45 under support doing 95 % of the work, an abrupt cut recovers, a taper over 5 periods recovers, and any taper longer than 9.13 periods traps the party.
